content: Thrombocytopenia, also known as thrombopenia, refers to a condition characterized by a reduced number of platelets in the blood. Normally, platelet counts range between 150,000 and 450,000 per mm³. However, deviations from this range do not necessarily indicate the presence of a disease. It is important to note that platelet counts in a blood sample can decrease rapidly over time, and a low count may sometimes result from delays between sample collection and analysis. Thrombocytopenia can be classified based on the severity of the platelet count. Mild thrombocytopenia is defined as a platelet count between 100,000 and 150,000 per µL, moderate thrombocytopenia ranges from 50,000 to 99,000 per µL, and severe thrombocytopenia is characterized by a count below 50,000 per µL. These thresholds, however, may vary depending on the underlying cause of thrombocytopenia. For instance, in idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), a platelet count below 30,000 per µL is considered severe, whereas in gestational thrombocytopenia, a count between 80,000 and 150,000 per µL is classified as mild. The pathophysiology of thrombocytopenia involves one or more of the following mechanisms: reduced platelet production due to bone marrow dysfunction, increased destruction of platelets within the body, iatrogenic causes, or sequestration of platelets in the spleen. Various conditions can activate these mechanisms, ultimately leading to thrombocytopenia. Among individuals with normal platelet counts, the mean platelet count is approximately 266,000 per µL in women and 237,000 per µL in men. Younger individuals and those of African-American descent tend to have higher platelet counts compared to older individuals and Caucasians, respectively. Platelet counts in a given individual remain relatively stable over time, with slight seasonal variations. For example, platelet counts are approximately 5,000 per µL higher in the fall and winter compared to the spring and summer. Additionally, about 5% of the normal population has platelet counts below 150,000 per µL.
